description: Replica PayPal account-closure page (the user has navigated to Settings → Profile → Close My Account). Deliberately injected dark patterns and counterexamples. Used to measure the identification prompt's true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative rates on a Finance & fintech fixture where the dominant DP signature is friction + hidden financial consequences.
page_url_when_served: http://localhost:8000/fixtures/paypal-account-close/paypal-account-close.html (or any http:// host; the extension rejects file:// URLs)

expected_page_evaluation.scoring_note: Mark page_evaluation correct if page_type ∈ {cancellation, settings, account_management} AND user_primary_intent is a reasonable paraphrase of 'close my PayPal account'. Vague intents ('manage my account', 'view settings') or wrong ones ('open new account', 'transfer money') are incorrect. The user came to close, the page is trying to talk them out of it. Every downstream harm test depends on this being correctly identified as a closure flow with close intent.

dark_patterns.element: 'What happens to your money and transactions' collapsed disclosure hiding pending-transaction force-close, recurring-payment failure cascade, dispute cancellation, balance-check mailing terms, 12-month reopen-blackout
dark_patterns.why: Decision-critical financial information buried in a collapsed, low-contrast disclosure (11px gray, no chevron): (a) pending transactions force-close with merchant-dispute risk to user's credit; (b) recurring payment authorizations to merchants begin failing silently — PayPal does not notify those merchants, who may forward unpaid invoices to collections; (c) any open buyer/seller dispute is cancelled with no refund; (d) the US$184.27 balance must be drained or PayPal mails a paper check (non-forwardable); (e) reopening the same email + tax ID combination is blocked for 12 months. A user who clicks close without expanding this loses material money + may incur knock-on financial consequences (credit impact, collections). Decision-critical financial info hidden at the moment of commitment. Canonical financial-account-close TOS-dump pattern.

dark_patterns.element: 'Keep My Account' giant blue pill button (full-width, 16px bold, PayPal brand blue #0070ba, 24px border-radius)
dark_patterns.why: The user navigated through 4 settings screens to GET to the close-account page. The visually dominant action in the action row is the KEEP pill (full-width, PayPal brand blue #0070ba, 16px bold, prominent pill border-radius), while the option that matches the user's revealed intent (close — see DP-3) is a tiny 11px gray underlined link below. Prominence misaligned with revealed user intent — the user already navigated through retention friction to get here; the dominant CTA reverses their action.

dark_patterns.element: Tiny gray close-account link below the Keep pill: 'Yes, close my account anyway and lose 14 years of transaction history, dispute protection, and my 1,247 verified Send-Money transactions'
dark_patterns.why: The close-account link's LABEL frames the user's choice as a self-inflicted loss enumerated in concrete personalized terms (14 years of history, dispute protection, 1,247 transactions — specific numbers fabricated for the fixture but the PATTERN of enumerating personalized losses is canonical financial-account language). The user can close (the link is functional), but the action option itself shames the user for the action by reciting every artifact they will lose. Manipulation is in the wording of the action control, not the action it performs. NOTE: this same element is also the visually-buried half of the False hierarchy pair with DP-2 (the KEEP pill) — a model that flags this link with type=False hierarchy is making a defensible call grounded in the same architectural pattern, hence the dual accepts_types.

counterexamples.element: 'Log Out' link in the top nav header
counterexamples.why_not: A standard navigation link present on every PayPal page. Nothing on this close-account page depends on the user logging out, and the link doesn't gate or coerce. Account-management nav affordances are routine.

counterexamples.element: Account summary card: current balance, pending count, last transaction, member-since date — all displayed openly
counterexamples.why_not: All decision-relevant account state (balance $184.27, 2 pending transactions, last activity date, account age) is visible up front in this card. Nothing collapsed, hidden, or buried. This is the OPPOSITE pattern of DP-1 (which hides post-closure financial consequences in a collapsed disclosure). The contrast pair (CE-2 vs DP-1) is a strong test of the model's harm-test reasoning: same financial-information surface, opposite harm-test answer based on what's revealed vs concealed at the decision moment.

counterexamples.element: Pre-checked 'Email me a confirmation when this completes' checkbox
counterexamples.why_not: A pre-checked checkbox inside the closure flow — but the option is a sensible one-shot transactional default: sending the user a record of an account-state change they just initiated. The receipt is one email, ends with closure, and provides a clear regulatory/financial paper trail (helpful for a banking-adjacent product). Not marketing, not a continuing subscription, not data extraction.

counterexamples.element: 'Need help? Visit our Customer Service center or call (888) 221-1161' link in the page footer
counterexamples.why_not: A footer help link is not coercive friction — it's an optional support affordance that the user can ignore entirely while completing closure. The harm test for Forced Action requires the user be FORCED to take an action; this link doesn't force anything.

fixture_notes: 3 DPs after the 2026-05 realism audit (issue #27). Originally 6 DPs; dropped 3 as not canonical for current PayPal close-account UX: dp-forced-reason (PayPal's reason picker is OPTIONAL in real UX, not a required gate — same caveat that retired Facebook's dp-forced-reason), dp-disguised-credit-promo (PayPal Credit is cross-promoted on shopping/checkout, not on close-account), dp-preselect-mailing-list (not a current PayPal close-flow opt-in).

The remaining 3 DPs are all canonical financial-account-close patterns: hidden post-closure financial consequences (DP-1 — TOS-dump shape), Keep pill dominance vs close link (DP-2), enumerate-the-loss close-link wording (DP-3).

DP-1 (hidden financial consequences) and CE-2 (balance summary shown openly) remain the most useful contrast pair on this fixture — same financial-information surface, opposite harm-test answer based on what's revealed vs concealed.

DP-3 (shame-link close) keeps multi-class accepts_types [Confirm shaming, False hierarchy] — same architectural element appears in both DP-2 (the pill-vs-link false-hierarchy pair) and DP-3 (the shame-label CS pattern). Convention established in netflix #14.
Disguised ad, Trick wording, Pop-up ad, Preselection, Fake social proof, and Forced Action have no coverage on this fixture by design — see issue #27 for the cross-fixture rationale.

scoring.true_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `dark_patterns` gt_id (by selector / html_evidence overlap) AND whose dark_pattern_type is in that entry's `accepts_types`.
scoring.false_negative: A `dark_patterns` gt_id has no matching entry in the model output.
scoring.false_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `counterexamples` gt_id, OR an entry whose target element matches no gt_id at all.
scoring.wrong_type: Model flags the right element (a `dark_patterns` gt_id) but with a dark_pattern_type NOT in `accepts_types`. Count separately from TP/FP — found something real but mislabeled it.
scoring.page_eval: Separately, score expected_page_evaluation as correct/incorrect per its scoring_note.
headline_metrics: recall = TP / (TP + FN)   [TP + FN = 3, the count of injected dark patterns post-audit]
false_positive_rate = FP / (number of counterexamples + extraneous flags) — this is the metric the recent prompt rewrite targets
Note: maxItems is 3 in the schema, so the model can report at most 3 patterns per run. Recall is no longer bounded by the schema cap on this fixture.
